cards.name: Tooth hypersensitivity or toothache
short: Hypersensitivity: open dentin tubules; a quick, sharp pain only while a stimulus (heat, cold, pressure, acid) is present. Toothache: bacterial invasion; the pain stays without a stimulus.
A toothache and severe pain are exclusions to self-care: nothing sold over the counter treats them and the dentist has to.
Order of treatment: soft-bristle toothbrush with standard fluoride toothpaste for 7 days; next, soft bristles with a desensitizing toothpaste.
Desensitizing actives: potassium nitrate 5% (not for children under 12), sodium fluoride, stannous fluoride, arginine 8%.
Counseling: 1-inch strip, at least twice daily, continuous use; dentist if pain persists, worsens or new symptoms appear after 4-6 weeks.

steps.title: Cause and timing: what makes the tooth hurt
steps.q: What exposes the dentin tubules, and what turns a stimulus into pain?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 7, 9, 14; handout pp. 2-3; T@45500, T@47772, T@48413 11/20

rows: {{Loss of enamel}} or {{gingival recession}} exposes dentin; the [[dentin-tubules|dentin tubules]] are open to both the oral cavity and the pulp (lesion initiation)
Heat, cold, pressure or acid make the fluid in the tubules expand and shrink, which stimulates the pulp nerve fibres (handout table)
Acidic juices and sodas; {{brushing too hard}}
Stomach acid that reaches the mouth {{erodes enamel}}; treating the reflux prevents further erosion. The handout adds: avoid large meals and acidic or spicy foods
Cause is bacterial invasion; the inflammatory response to the bacteria stimulates free nerve endings in the pulp

steps.title: Recognise it: hypersensitivity or toothache
steps.q: Which feature separates tooth hypersensitivity from toothache?
steps.src: Lam oral slide 9; handout pp. 2-3; T@46304, T@55389-T@56012 11/20

rows: A {{quick, fleeting, sharp or stabbing}} pain on exposure to thermal, chemical or physical stimuli; it {{stops}} after the stimulus is gone
Pain that {{remains even in the absence of a stimulus}}
Intermittent, short, sharp pain on stimulation may indicate reversible damage; continuous, dull, throbbing pain without stimulation usually indicates irreversible damage
The patient's own description (subjective). She said she will write {{very severe}} on the exam when the pain is a reason to see the dentist

items: She teaches the difference as: pain that occurs when the tooth is exposed to something (hypersensitivity) versus constant pain whatever the patient does (toothache).

steps.title: Self-care or refer?
steps.q: Name five exclusions to self-care and the follow-up time for a patient who is treated.

items: {{Toothache}}
Fever or swelling
Trauma to the mouth with bleeding, swelling and soreness
{{Loose teeth}}; broken or knocked-out teeth
{{Bleeding gums}}
Severe tooth pain triggered or worsened by hot, cold or chewing
Mouth soreness associated with poor-fitting dentures

rows: Why a toothache is an exclusion
Nothing sold over the counter treats bacterial invasion; the dentist has to clean it out
She said it usually means so much gum recession that the dentist must do a deep cleaning, which a pharmacist cannot do
Repair the damaged tooth surface with the appropriate toothpaste; minimize abrasion
If pain persists or worsens, or new symptoms develop after {{4-6 weeks}} (slide 18). She said "after 4 weeks" aloud (T@50822)
She said everyone should see a dentist at least every {{6 months}}

steps.title: Treat it: the guideline order
steps.q: What is the first step, what is the next step, and which ingredient is not for children under 12?

items: Eliminate predisposing factors: acidic food and drinks, brushing too hard
Avoid brushing for {{30-60 minutes}} after acidic food or drinks
Use a low-abrasion toothbrush with standard fluoride toothpaste
Minimize GERD symptoms

blocks.label: First
blocks.title: Soft-bristle toothbrush + standard fluoride toothpaste for 7 days
pts: {{7 days}}: the first step for a patient who is not already doing it
Fluoride toothpaste helps the enamel surface; she said that is all it does
She said practice often skips this step, but the guideline she cited recommends it first
pick: Acid drinks every day and a hard brush
Change the habits and the brush first; no desensitizing product yet (her 26-year-old case: "Not yet")
Already on a soft brush and standard fluoride
blocks.move: Move to the next line when: the soft-bristle brush with standard fluoride has been used and the pain is not better after one week (T@54083).

blocks.label: Next
blocks.title: Soft-bristle brush + desensitizing toothpaste
pts: {{Depolarizes the excited nerves in the tubules}}: potassium nitrate 5%, sodium fluoride, stannous fluoride
{{Seals the exposed dentin}} so less fluid flows: arginine 8% (the handout writes arginine calcium)
Choose by the active ingredient: she gives no brand names because brands change and carry different ingredients
blocks.warn: Potassium nitrate 5%: not for children under 12 years; children swallow toothpaste, with a higher risk of electrolyte problems.
pick: Read the active ingredient on the label
blocks.move: Refer to a dentist when: pain persists or worsens, or new symptoms develop after 4-6 weeks.

rows: A single application has no effect; it needs {{continuous use}}
Apply a {{1-inch}} strip to a soft-bristle brush and brush at least {{twice daily}}
Long-term use to relieve the symptoms: the handout says over 4-6 weeks; she said 4 to 6 weeks to see the benefit
Continue until the sensitivity subsides or as long as the dentist recommends

steps.title: Fluoride and the chemistry of the tooth products (Dr. Sikazwe)
steps.q: How does fluoride protect enamel, and what do the non-fluoride products do?
steps.src: Sikazwe OOO slides 15-21 (assigned); slides 22-24 not on his assigned pages

rows: Bacteria form plaque on teeth and gums; bacteria convert sugars into acids that erode enamel and lead to cavities; acid drinks also erode enamel; smoking alters saliva pH and promotes bacterial growth; substance use (meth, crack cocaine)

Enamel's {{hydroxyapatite}} is vulnerable to acid erosion. Fluoride ions from toothpastes or gels (Na2PO3F, SnF2, NaF) convert it into [[fluorapatite|fluorapatite]], Ca10(PO4)6F2, which resists acid erosion, and they enhance mineral deposition
More than {{2 mg/L}} can cause enamel fluorosis (slide 18)

Sodium bicarbonate: an abrasive and mouth pH elevating agent. Nanohydroxyapatite (10% nHA): crystals of 50-1000 nm that bond to hydroxyapatite. Calcium sodium phosphosilicate: a bioactive glass that deposits crystalline hydroxycarbonate apatite. Amorphous calcium phosphate: releases Ca2+ and PO4 ions on contact with saliva to remineralize enamel

Fluoride: promotes remineralization and prevents caries. NaHCO3: raises saliva pH and lowers growth of acidic bacteria. Chlorhexidine gluconate (a biguanide salt) and cetylpyridinium chloride (a pyridinium salt) are cationic: they bind the bacterial cell wall electrostatically and their lipophilic tails disrupt it

Slide 22: amalgam fillings are less common because of environmental and toxicity concerns. Slide 23: the most common resin is Bis-GMA, a polymer of bisphenol A and glycidyl methacrylate. Slide 24: whiteners range from H2O2 (oxidizes stains) to abrasives to surfactants

patients.t: Mr. Alvarez, 61, has throbbing pain in a back tooth. It started three days ago and nothing makes it better or worse. His GERD is controlled with an OTC acid reducer, and he brushes once a day with a regular toothbrush.
patients.q: What is the most appropriate intervention?
o: Counsel him on minimizing his GERD symptoms
A soft-bristle toothbrush with standard fluoride toothpaste
A toothpaste that contains potassium nitrate 5%
A referral to a dentist
patients.w: Throbbing pain that continues without a stimulus is a toothache from bacterial invasion. A toothache is an exclusion: nothing sold over the counter helps and the dentist has to clean it out (slides 9, 11; T@51849 11/20).

x.Counsel him on minimizing his GERD sympt: GERD erodes enamel, but his pain is constant and not triggered; this does not treat a toothache.
x.A soft-bristle toothbrush with standard: This is the first step for hypersensitivity, which needs a stimulus; his pain has none.
x.A toothpaste that contains potassium nit: A desensitizing toothpaste treats open dentin tubules, not a bacterial toothache.

patients.t: Ms. Rivera, 30, has a short, sharp tooth pain when she drinks hot or cold drinks. It is mild and started two days ago. She drinks lemonade with lunch and orange juice with breakfast, and brushes twice a day with a medium-bristle toothbrush and fluoride toothpaste. A dentist saw her a month ago with no concerns.
patients.q: What is the best first recommendation?
o: Start a desensitizing toothpaste with potassium nitrate 5% right away
Use a stannous fluoride desensitizing toothpaste with her medium brush
Cut back on acidic drinks and use a soft brush with standard fluoride
Return to her dentist today because the pain started two days ago
patients.w: Her pain needs a stimulus, so it is hypersensitivity, and she has no exclusion. The first step is to remove the acid exposure and the abrasion with a soft-bristle brush and standard fluoride for 7 days; a desensitizing toothpaste comes only after that (slides 14, 15, 22; T@53195-T@54367 11/20).

x.Start a desensitizing toothpaste with po: A desensitizing toothpaste is the next step, after one week of the first step.
x.Use a stannous fluoride desensitizing to: Stannous fluoride is a desensitizing product, which comes after the first step, and the medium brush adds abrasion.
x.Return to her dentist today because the: Mild pain with a stimulus and a recent normal dental visit is not an exclusion.

patients.t: Ms. Chen, 24, used a soft-bristle brush and standard fluoride toothpaste for 9 days and stopped her acidic drinks. She still has a sharp pain with cold air. It is mild, and she has no swelling.
o: Repeat the same soft-brush step for another full week
Refer her to a dentist now because the first step did not work
Switch to a firmer brush so the teeth are cleaned better
Add a desensitizing toothpaste such as one with arginine 8%
patients.w: The first step has been done for more than a week without relief and she has no exclusion, so the next line is a soft-bristle brush with a desensitizing toothpaste (slide 15; T@54083 11/20).

x.Repeat the same soft-brush step for anot: The first step is 7 days; she has already finished it.
x.Refer her to a dentist now because the f: Referral is for exclusions, or pain that persists or worsens after 4-6 weeks of the desensitizing toothpaste.
x.Switch to a firmer brush so the teeth ar: A firmer brush adds abrasion; one treatment goal is to minimize abrasion.

patients.t: A father asks which desensitizing toothpaste to buy for his 11-year-old, who has mild pain with cold drinks and has finished the first step.
patients.q: Which active ingredient is not recommended for this child?
o: Sodium fluoride
Potassium nitrate 5%
Stannous fluoride
Arginine 8%
patients.w: Potassium nitrate is not for children under 12 years because children swallow toothpaste, with a higher risk of electrolyte problems (slide 15; T@50194 11/20).

x.Sodium fluoride: Sodium fluoride is one of the listed desensitizing ingredients and carries no age limit on the slide.
x.Stannous fluoride: Stannous fluoride carries no age limit on the slide.
x.Arginine 8%: Arginine 8% carries no age limit on the slide.

patients.t: Mr. Davis, 47, has a sharp pain with cold drinks. He also has bleeding gums and a loose lower tooth.
o: A desensitizing toothpaste with sodium fluoride
A hydrogen peroxide rinse for the gums
A soft-bristle brush with standard fluoride for 7 days
A referral to a dentist
patients.w: Bleeding gums and loose teeth are exclusions to self-care (slide 11); nothing OTC treats them.

x.A desensitizing toothpaste with sodium f: A desensitizing toothpaste does not treat bleeding gums or a loose tooth, which are exclusions.
x.A hydrogen peroxide rinse for the gums: A peroxide rinse is a canker sore product and can irritate teeth and soft tissue.
x.A soft-bristle brush with standard fluor: The first step is for patients without an exclusion.

patients.t: A patient has used a desensitizing toothpaste twice daily for 5 weeks. The cold pain is unchanged and a new burning area has appeared on the gum.
o: Use a 2-inch strip of toothpaste each time
Continue the same toothpaste for 4 more weeks
Refer to a dentist for further evaluation
Stop the toothpaste and use ice on the gum
patients.w: Pain that persists, and new symptoms after 4-6 weeks, are the reasons to refer to a dentist (slide 18). A 1-inch strip is enough (T@50656 11/20).

x.Use a 2-inch strip of toothpaste each ti: She said 1 inch is enough; more paste does not add effect.
x.Continue the same toothpaste for 4 more: Pain that persists after 4-6 weeks is the point to refer, not to extend.
x.Stop the toothpaste and use ice on the g: Ice is advice for a canker sore, and a new gum symptom needs evaluation.

numbers: soft-bristle brush with standard fluoride toothpaste, the first step
wait before brushing after acidic food or drinks
potassium nitrate in a desensitizing toothpaste
strip of toothpaste, at least twice daily
long-term use; dentist if pain persists or new symptoms appear
fluoride above this can cause enamel fluorosis

cards.name: Canker sore (recurrent aphthous stomatitis)
short: Gray or yellowish oval ulcer with a red halo on the lining inside the mouth; the exact cause is unknown, so triggers are listed.
It heals by itself in 7-14 days; the goals are pain relief and preventing complications.
Refer if the lesion lasts over 14 days, recurs often, comes with systemic illness, or earlier self-care failed.
No product is first: topical anesthetic, debriding agent, protectant, rinse and systemic analgesic can each be used; she will ask for counseling on the product chosen.
Debriding agents: after meals, wait 30 minutes, at most 7 days (black hairy tongue). Ice, not heat.

steps.title: Cause and timing
steps.q: Is the cause known, and what are the five groups of precipitating factors?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 26, 27; handout p. 5; T@57025-T@59651 11/20

rows: The exact cause is {{unknown}}; known triggers cause it
Smoking, chemical irritation, biting the inside of the cheeks or lips, injury from toothbrushing or braces
HIV/AIDS, inflammatory bowel diseases; she said a lowered immune system raises the chance
Gluten-sensitive enteropathy; deficiencies in {{iron}}, {{B vitamins}} and {{folic acid}}; she named celiac disease and short bowel syndrome
Antibiotics, antiepileptics, diuretics, chemotherapy, antiretrovirals, anti-inflammatory drugs
Genetic and allergic factors, stress, hormonal changes, food
It resolves on its own in {{7-14 days}}

steps.title: Recognise it
steps.q: Where does a canker sore appear, what does it look like, and what comes first?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 27, 47; handout pp. 5, 9; T@57025-T@59261 11/20

rows: Non-keratinized mucosa of the movable mouth: tongue, floor of the mouth, soft palate, inside the lips and cheeks
Round or oval ulcers; flat or crateriform (crater-like center); {{gray or grayish yellow}} with an {{erythematous halo}} of inflamed tissue
Some patients feel a pricking or burning sensation, a [[prodrome|prodrome]], about {{2-48 hours}} before the lesion appears
Pain that increases with eating and drinking; normal activities may be severely limited
Oval, flat ulcer with erythematous tissue around it; all areas except the gingiva, hard palate and vermilion border
Oval, ragged, gray or yellow, crateriform ulcers; lips, soft palate and throat
Small oval ulcers in crops, similar to minor RAS; any intraoral area

steps.title: Self-care or refer?
steps.q: Name five exclusions to self-care and the three treatment-failure referral times.

items: Lesions associated with underlying pathology
Lesions present {{more than 14 days}}: something else may be causing them
Frequently recurring lesions: look for a cause such as a nutritional deficiency
Symptoms of systemic illness: inflamed lymph nodes, fever, signs of infection
Failure of prior appropriate self-care treatment

rows: {{Pain relief}} and {{prevent complications}}, such as secondary infection; the handout adds deterring recurrence
Symptoms do not abate after {{7 days}} of treatment with oral debriding or wound-cleansing agents
The lesions do not heal in {{14 days}}
Is the patient a candidate for self-care, or does the patient need a healthcare provider? Then: given this product, what are the key counseling points? She will not ask which product comes first

steps.title: Treat it: match the product to the need
steps.q: Which products relieve pain, which clean the sore, and what is the main counseling point for each?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 32-39; handout pp. 6-8; T@61228-T@69948 11/20; Sikazwe OOO slide 20

items: Avoid spicy, acidic and sharp-textured food
Ice, not heat: {{10-minute}} periods, no longer than {{20 minutes}} in each hour; heat may spread the infection
Deter recurrence: eat more nutritious food if the cause is a nutritional deficiency

blocks.label: Pain
blocks.title: Topical anesthetic: benzocaine or benzyl alcohol
pts: Gives temporary relief of pain; benzocaine {{10-20%}} and benzyl alcohol {{0.05-0.1%}} on slide 34
Apply to the sore up to {{4 times}} a day as needed (handout: age over 2 years)
Do not combine with menthol, phenol or camphor: tissue irritation and damage; she named lozenges, throat sprays and Vicks products as menthol sources
blocks.warn: The handout prints benzocaine 5-20%, the slide 10-20%; she gave no number.

blocks.label: Clean
blocks.title: Oral debriding and wound-cleansing agent
pts: Cleanses the mouth to prevent infection and gives symptomatic relief; carbamide peroxide {{10-15%}}, hydrogen peroxide {{1.5%}} or {{3%}}
Use after meals, 3-4 times a day; avoid eating or drinking for at least {{30 minutes}} after
Use for up to {{7 days}}: over-cleaning lets opportunistic organisms grow, causing black hairy tongue; prolonged use also causes tooth sensitivity and soft tissue irritation
Patient with sensitive teeth: use direct application to the sore, not the rinse
blocks.warn: She said carbamide peroxide direct application sits 1 or 2 minutes; the slide and handout say 1 minute.
facts: Carbamide peroxide, direct application: apply to the area, leave 1 minute, spit
Carbamide peroxide, rinse: a few drops on the tongue, mix with saliva, swish 1 minute
Hydrogen peroxide 1.5%: direct application, 1 minute, spit
Hydrogen peroxide 3%: swish for one minute (handout: mixed with an equal amount of water first)

blocks.label: Coat
blocks.title: Topical oral protectant (paste, patch or disc)
pts: Coats and protects the sore so it is not irritated; a barrier forms and dissolves in {{8-12 hours}}
Use up to 3-4 times a day after meals; avoid drinking for up to 30 minutes so the patch adheres
blocks.warn: Placement time of the disc: slide 37 prints 10-20 seconds; the handout and her speech say 10-20 minutes.

blocks.label: Rinse
blocks.title: Saline rinse or baking soda paste
pts: Hastens healing and soothes the ulcers; use up to {{4 times}} a day
Saline: 1-3 teaspoons of salt in 4-8 ounces of warm water; any salt
Baking soda paste: apply to the lesion for a few minutes
The guideline gives no order: any of these products can be tried first, based on the patient's schedule or choice

blocks.label: Extra pain relief
blocks.title: Systemic analgesic
pts: NSAIDs or acetaminophen for additional relief
Aspirin is not held in the mouth: chemical burn

rows: Used as a mouth rinse for canker sores
An anesthetic agent in gels or combination agents; methemoglobinemia is rare but a concern: CYP enzymes convert benzocaine to benzocaine hydroxylamine, which causes it

steps.title: Follow up
steps.q: When does a canker sore resolve, and when does the patient go to a provider?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 40; handout p. 8; T@69759-T@70079 11/20

items: Minor lesions are self-limiting and resolve within {{14 days}}; if symptoms resolve, stop the treatment
Symptoms still present after 7 days of debriding or cleansing agents: refer
Lesions not healed in 14 days: refer
Symptoms worse during self-treatment, or fever, rash or swelling: refer

patients.t: Ms. Park, 28, is stressed from exams. She has a gray-yellow oval ulcer with a red rim inside her lower lip. It is painful when she eats. She felt burning there the day before it appeared.
o: Canker sore (recurrent aphthous stomatitis)
Cold sore (herpes simplex labialis) on the lip
Toothache from bacterial invasion of the tooth
Tooth hypersensitivity from exposed dentin tubules
patients.w: A gray or yellow oval ulcer with a red halo inside the mouth, preceded by burning (a prodrome), is a canker sore. A cold sore is red, fluid-filled and on or around the lip (slides 27, 47).

x.Cold sore (herpes simplex labialis) on t: A cold sore is a red, fluid-filled lesion outside the mouth at the lip and skin junction.
x.Toothache from bacterial invasion of the: A toothache is a deep tooth pain that remains without a stimulus, not an ulcer.
x.Tooth hypersensitivity from exposed dent: Hypersensitivity is a sharp pain on exposure to a stimulus, without a mouth ulcer.

patients.t: A man has had a painful ulcer on his cheek lining for 3 weeks. He has tried a benzocaine gel and a saline rinse without relief.
o: Hydrogen peroxide 3% rinse for 7 more days
A protectant disc after meals
Referral to his PCP
Baking soda paste for a few minutes
patients.w: Lesions present more than 14 days, and failure of prior self-care, are exclusions to self-care (slide 29).

x.Hydrogen peroxide 3% rinse for 7 more da: A debriding agent is limited to 7 days and does not fit a lesion over 14 days.
x.A protectant disc after meals: A protectant is a self-care product; he has two exclusions.
x.Baking soda paste for a few minutes: Baking soda paste is a self-care rinse; self-care has failed.

patients.t: A patient chooses hydrogen peroxide for a canker sore.
o: Swish and swallow it with water after each meal so it keeps working
Use it for 3 weeks to keep the sore clean until it heals
Spit it out after each use and wait 30 minutes before eating
Hold it in the mouth for 10 minutes after each use of it
patients.w: Debriding agents are used after meals 3-4 times a day, spit out, followed by 30 minutes without food or drink, for up to 7 days (slides 35-36).

x.Swish and swallow it with water after ea: The product is spit out, not swallowed.
x.Use it for 3 weeks to keep the sore clea: Use is limited to 7 days; longer use can cause black hairy tongue.

patients.t: A patient with a canker sore also has sensitive teeth. She asks how to use hydrogen peroxide.
o: Swish a 3% rinse twice as long to protect the teeth
Use direct application on the sore, not the rinse
Mix it with her toothpaste and brush
Use the rinse with ice in the mouth
patients.w: Hydrogen peroxide can irritate enamel and soft tissue; she said patients with sensitive teeth should use the applicator and not the rinse (T@65066, T@67096 11/20).

x.Swish a 3% rinse twice as long to protec: A longer swish increases the exposure, and prolonged use causes tooth sensitivity.
x.Mix it with her toothpaste and brush: Mixing it into toothpaste is not a described use.
x.Use the rinse with ice in the mouth: Ice is non-drug care for pain, not a way to use a peroxide rinse.

patients.t: A man with a canker sore uses a benzocaine gel and a camphor-menthol rub on the same sore.
o: Keep both because the two together relieve pain better
Use the rub first and the gel second to lower irritation
Keep both but use them only before meals
Stop combining them: it irritates and damages tissue
patients.w: Benzocaine and benzyl alcohol are not combined with menthol, phenol or camphor because of tissue irritation (slide 34).

x.Keep both because the two together relie: The combination irritates the tissue; it does not add relief.
x.Use the rub first and the gel second to: The order does not remove the irritation.
x.Keep both but use them only before meals: The problem is the combination, not the timing.

patients.t: A patient asks what to do at home for a painful canker sore, without a product.
o: Apply heat for 20 minutes in each hour to relax the area
Apply ice in 10-minute periods, up to 20 minutes in each hour
Eat spicy food so that the sore gets cleaned out
Apply ice for 30 minutes at a time until the pain stops
patients.w: Ice reduces swelling in 10-minute periods, up to 20 minutes in each hour; heat may spread the infection (handout p. 6; T@61228 11/20).

x.Apply heat for 20 minutes in each hour t: Heat is avoided because it may spread the infection.
x.Eat spicy food so that the sore gets cle: Spicy, acidic and sharp foods irritate the sore.
x.Apply ice for 30 minutes at a time until: Ice is limited to 10-minute periods and 20 minutes in each hour.

numbers: a canker sore resolves on its own
maximum use of a debriding agent; refer if not better
no eating or drinking after a product
ice, at a time and in each hour
most products: up to 3-4 times a day after meals

cards.name: Cold sore (herpes simplex labialis)
short: Herpes simplex virus 1: contagious by direct contact, then latent and reactivated by triggers (stress, sun, wind, cold, fever, injury).
It starts with tingling or burning, then red fluid-filled vesicles that merge and crust, on or around the lip.
Exclusions: no previous diagnosis, more than 14 days, increased frequency, immunocompromised, systemic signs, recurrence.
First line: docosanol 10% at the first sign, up to 5 times a day until healed, up to 10 days; a topical anesthetic is optional for pain.
Not recommended: topical steroids; tea tree oil, lysine and zinc have too little data.

steps.title: Cause and timing
steps.q: What causes a cold sore, how is it spread, and what triggers it?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 43, 44; handout pp. 8-9; T@70941-T@72227 11/20

rows: Herpes simplex virus 1 ({{HSV-1}}); HSV-2 is associated with genital sores (infectious disease module)
Contagious by {{direct contact}}; fluid in the vesicles holds live virus, which stays viable on surfaces for several hours
The virus becomes [[latency|latent]] and reactivates when a stimulus triggers it
Ultraviolet light, stress, fatigue, cold, windburn, fever, injury, menstruation, dental work, infectious diseases and other factors that suppress the immune system

steps.title: Recognise it: the stages
steps.q: What are the stages of a cold sore, and where is it located?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 45, 47; handout p. 9; T@72227-T@73857 11/20

rows: Slide 47: junction of oral mucosa and skin of the lip and nose. She said outside the mouth, on or around the lips
{{2-48 hours}} of burning, itching, tingling or numbness; other signs may be pain, fever, localized bleeding, swollen lymph nodes and malaise
Small red papules of fluid-containing [[or-vesicle|vesicles]], 1-3 mm in diameter; many merge into a larger area; an erythematous, inflamed border
A {{crust}} often forms over the coalesced, burst vesicles; the base stays erythematous
The crust never forms, or the erythematous border persists

steps.title: Self-care or refer?
steps.q: Which exclusions apply, and what counts as recurrence in her cases?

items: {{No previous diagnosis}} of a cold sore: the pharmacist has no scope to diagnose it
Lesions present {{more than 14 days}}
Increased frequency of outbreaks
{{Immunocompromised}}
Symptoms of systemic infection (fever, swollen lymph nodes, rash)
Recurrence

rows: Slide 49 prints "recurrence" without a time. She called an outbreak {{once a month}} reoccurring. Her second case, a lesion {{a year}} after the last outbreak and already seen by a provider, is a self-care candidate
Reduce the duration of the active infection; relieve pain and irritation while the sores heal; prevent secondary infection; curtail the spread
Avoid triggers: stress, fatigue, wind, excessive sun, local trauma
Sun exposure: sunscreen on the face and lips; the handout adds an SPF lip protectant
Keep the skin moist to prevent drying and cracking: cracks make a secondary infection easier
Keep lesions clean with gentle washing with mild soap, and wash the hands often
The lesions do not heal in {{14 days}}
Fever, malaise, rash or swollen lymph glands

steps.title: Treat it: antiviral first, analgesic added
steps.q: What is the first-line product and how is it used, and what is not recommended?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 51-58; handout pp. 10-12; T@77492-T@81994 11/20

blocks.label: First
blocks.title: Docosanol 10% cream (Abreva)
pts: Topical antiviral: {{reduces the duration and the severity}} of symptoms, so it is first line
Mechanism: it prevents the herpesvirus from fusing with the human cell plasma membrane, so the virus does not replicate
Apply at the {{first sign}} (the prodrome); it works best before the lesion appears but still helps afterwards
Up to {{5 times}} a day until the lesion heals, for up to {{10 days}}
pick: Tingling or burning, no lesion yet

blocks.label: Plus or minus
blocks.title: Topical analgesic or anesthetic
pts: Relieves burning, itching and pain; it {{does not reduce the duration}} of the infection
Apply a thin layer after meals, 3-4 times a day; avoid eating or drinking for at least 30 minutes
Camphor above {{3%}} and menthol above {{1%}} are contraindicated: counterirritant effect; Vicks rub has about 5% camphor
facts: Benzocaine 5-20% (adults and children 2 years and older)

blocks.label: Pain
blocks.title: Systemic analgesic
pts: Aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen or acetaminophen for pain only
Aspirin is not held on the lesion

blocks.label: Secondary infection
blocks.title: Triple antibiotic ointment
pts: Only if the lesion is not forming a mature lesion: no crust and still red
Thin layer {{3-4 times}} a day; the patient follows up with the PCP

items: <<topical-steroid-hsl|Topical steroids>>: the herpes virus does not respond to corticosteroids, and they are [[or-astringent|highly astringent]], which irritates the skin
<<complementary-hsl|Tea tree oil, lysine and zinc>>: not enough data; the guidelines do not recommend them to prevent or treat cold sores

steps.title: Follow up
steps.q: How long does a cold sore take to heal, and when does the patient go to the PCP?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 59, 60; handout p. 12; T@81994-T@82500 11/20

items: Cold sores are self-limiting; healing occurs within {{10-14 days}}
If symptoms have resolved, no further treatment is necessary
Refer for: no healing in 14 days, recurrence despite appropriate self-care, no relief, signs of systemic illness, changing or worsening symptoms

patients.t: A 42-year-old woman has an uncomfortable sore on her lip. She gets these often when she is stressed, about once a month. This one has been there for a month. It is crusted with fluid-filled pustules.
patients.q: Is she a candidate for self-care?
o: Yes, start docosanol 10% five times a day
No, the lesion has lasted over 14 days and the outbreaks recur
No, because a lip sore is always a canker sore
Yes, with hydrocortisone 1% ointment as needed
patients.w: Lesions present more than 14 days, and frequent recurrence (she counted once a month as reoccurring), are exclusions (slide 49; T@83053-T@83449 11/20).

x.Yes, start docosanol 10% five times a da: Docosanol is first line, but she has exclusions.
x.No, because a lip sore is always a canke: A canker sore is inside the mouth; her lesion is on the lip, crusted and fluid-filled.
x.Yes, with hydrocortisone 1% ointment as: The herpes virus does not respond to corticosteroids.

patients.t: A 21-year-old has a painful, small, red lesion outside the lower lip. Cold, windy weather always brings her outbreaks. Her last cold sore was a year ago, and the campus wellness center said she can use something over the counter. She takes a birth control pill.
patients.q: Is she a candidate for self-care?
o: No, any recurrence at all is an exclusion to self-care
No, because she takes a birth control pill every day
Yes, because she cannot have any prior diagnosis of cold sores
Yes, an infrequent outbreak that a provider has already seen
patients.w: Her last outbreak was a year ago, which she did not count as reoccurring, and she already saw a provider. She is a candidate (T@83449-T@83700 11/20).

x.No, any recurrence at all is an exclusio: Slide 49 lists recurrence, but she called monthly outbreaks reoccurring, not one a year.
x.No, because she takes a birth control pi: Nothing on the slides excludes the patient for a birth control pill.
x.Yes, because she cannot have any prior d: No previous diagnosis is the exclusion; she has a history of HSL.

patients.t: The same 21-year-old needs a recommendation.
o: Hydrocortisone 1% ointment as needed for the inflammation
Camphor 5% gel 3-4 times a day after meals for the pain
Docosanol 10% five times a day until healed
Tea tree oil and lysine taken together every day
patients.w: Docosanol 10% five times a day until healed is first line (slide 53). Steroids do not act on the virus, camphor above 3% is contraindicated, and tea tree oil, lysine and zinc have too little data (slides 54, 57, 58).

x.Hydrocortisone 1% ointment as needed for: The herpes virus does not respond to corticosteroids, and they are highly astringent.
x.Tea tree oil and lysine taken together e: The guidelines do not recommend these for cold sores.

patients.t: A man on day 5 of a cold sore has a lesion that has not crusted. The base and border are still red.
patients.q: What do you recommend in addition?
o: Hydrocortisone 1% ointment applied twice a day to the lesion
Triple antibiotic ointment 3-4 times a day and PCP follow-up
Camphor 5% gel applied after each meal to the lesion
Hold an aspirin tablet against the sore until it dissolves
patients.w: No crust with persistent redness points to a secondary infection. Triple antibiotic ointment is used 3-4 times a day with PCP follow-up (slides 45, 56).

x.Hydrocortisone 1% ointment applied twice: Steroids are not recommended for cold sores.
x.Camphor 5% gel applied after each meal t: Camphor above 3% is contraindicated and does not treat infection.
x.Hold an aspirin tablet against the sore: Aspirin held in the mouth or on the lesion causes a chemical burn.

patients.t: A woman has never had a cold sore. She has a painful lip lesion, a fever and swollen lymph nodes.
o: Docosanol 10% five times a day
A benzocaine gel after meals
A triple antibiotic ointment
Referral to her PCP
patients.w: No previous diagnosis of a cold sore and symptoms of systemic infection are both exclusions (slide 49). She said a pharmacist has no scope to diagnose a first cold sore.

x.Docosanol 10% five times a day: Docosanol is for a patient who qualifies for self-care.
x.A benzocaine gel after meals: An anesthetic treats pain only; she has exclusions.
x.A triple antibiotic ointment: Triple antibiotic ointment is for a suspected secondary infection in a self-care patient.

patients.t: A man feels burning and tingling at the corner of his lip. There is no blister yet. He has had cold sores before and has no exclusions.
o: Now, at the first sign
When the vesicles appear
When the crust forms
After 3 days of symptoms
patients.w: Docosanol works best when applied at the first sign, before the lesion occurs (slide 53; T@78879 11/20).

x.When the vesicles appear: It still helps once the lesion appears but works best before it.
x.When the crust forms: Waiting until crusting loses the time when it works best.
x.After 3 days of symptoms: She said the earlier it is applied, the better.

numbers: docosanol: use for up to 10 days
above these, contraindicated in a cold sore
topical anesthetic or triple antibiotic ointment

cards.name: Dry mouth (xerostomia)
short: [[xerostomia|Xerostomia]]: often caused by medicines with anticholinergic activity or that deplete salivary flow, by radiation to the head and neck, and by some diseases.
It increases the risk of cavities and causes bad breath and thrush.
The goal: remove the offending medicine or condition if possible, relieve the discomfort and reduce the risk of dental decay.
Artificial saliva is replacement therapy, not a cure; sodium-containing products are avoided on a low-sodium diet.
Re-evaluate after 5-7 days; dryness worse or new symptoms: refer.

steps.title: Cause and timing: risk factors
steps.q: Which medicine classes and conditions can cause dry mouth, and by which two mechanisms?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 72-75; handout pp. 13-14; T@86106-T@87063 11/20

rows: A medicine has {{anticholinergic}} activity, or it {{depletes salivary flow volume}}
Antihistamines, decongestants, antihypertensives, diuretics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, sedatives

Diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, oxybutynin, solifenacin, clonidine, long-acting muscarinic antagonists (tiotropium), haloperidol, risperidone, mirtazapine, bupropion, atomoxetine, duloxetine, venlafaxine, citalopram, trazodone, guanfacine
Sjögren's syndrome (an autoimmune condition in which the salivary glands are partly or entirely dysfunctional), diabetes mellitus, depression, Crohn's disease
Radiation therapy of the head and neck; older patients on multiple medicines
She confirmed diphenhydramine, tiotropium, clonidine and citalopram as medicines that can cause dry mouth; bupropion is in the handout list

steps.title: Recognise it
steps.q: What are the signs and complications of dry mouth?
steps.src: Lam oral slide 76; handout p. 13; T@87063-T@87494 11/20

items: Difficulty talking, chewing and swallowing
Stomatitis; dry lips
Plaque accumulation
{{Halitosis}} (bad breath); loss of appetite and sense of taste
Increased risk of dental {{caries}}; the handout adds periodontal disease despite good oral hygiene
{{Thrush}}

steps.title: Self-care or refer?
steps.q: What are the goals, and when is the patient not a candidate?

rows: Slide 78: relieve the discomfort of dry mouth; reduce the risk of dental decay. Handout and speech add: remove the offending medicine or condition if possible
Exclusions (slide 79; she did not read them aloud)
Sjögren's syndrome or a salivary gland stone
Bleeding and swelling, with or without trauma
Loose teeth, or tooth erosion or decay
Mouth soreness from poor-fitting dentures, or reduced denture wearing time
Severe tooth pain triggered or worsened by hot, cold or chewing

Slide 84 and her speech: dryness that worsens, or new symptoms or complications, go to the {{PCP}} to find the cause. The handout (p. 15) says referral to dental for further evaluation. Both are stated

steps.title: Treat it: remove the cause, then relieve
steps.q: What non-drug steps help, and how is artificial saliva used?
steps.src: Lam oral slides 81-84; handout pp. 14-15; T@87494-T@90547 11/20; Sikazwe OOO slide 17

blocks.text: Remove the offending agent or condition (slide 81)

items: Stop medicines and substances that reduce salivation where possible: tobacco (smoked and smokeless), alcohol including mouth rinses, caffeine, hot spicy foods
If a medicine contributes and cannot be stopped: take it {{1 hour before meals}}, because eating stimulates saliva (T@88526)
Maintain oral hygiene: brush twice a day and see the dentist
Chew {{sugar-free gum}} (xylitol): it stimulates the salivary glands
Increase water intake, especially if fluoridated
A humidifier adds moisture to the air
A very soft toothbrush minimizes tissue abrasion

blocks.label: Replace
blocks.title: Artificial saliva
pts: {{Replacement therapy, not a cure}}: it lacks the protective components of the natural saliva
Sprays, gels, gums and toothpaste; gel: place a {{1/2-inch}} length on the tongue and spread it through the mouth
Use at any time: at a minimum after all meals and before going to bed
Patient on a {{low-sodium diet}}: avoid products that contain sodium (sodium carboxymethylcellulose, sodium monofluorophosphate)
pick: Heart failure or a sodium-restricted diet
Continue artificial saliva, fluoride products and the non-drug measures
blocks.move: Refer when: dryness becomes worse, or additional symptoms or complications develop.

patients.t: Mr. Lewis, 70, has had a dry mouth for 3 weeks. He takes diphenhydramine each night for sleep and has a dry throat and dry lips.
patients.q: What best explains his dry mouth?
o: Diphenhydramine has anticholinergic activity
His fluoride toothpaste is drying the saliva out
Humidity in his bedroom is drying out the mouth
A salivary gland stone caused by his age
patients.w: Antihistamines such as diphenhydramine have anticholinergic activity and reduce salivation (slide 72; T@86106-T@86368 11/20).

x.His fluoride toothpaste is drying the sa: Fluoride products are used to lower dental decay risk in dry mouth; they do not cause it.
x.Humidity in his bedroom is drying out th: A humidifier is a measure that relieves dry mouth.
x.A salivary gland stone caused by his age: A stone is an exclusion for self-care, but nothing in the case points to one.

patients.t: A woman is stable on an antipsychotic that causes her dry mouth. Her prescriber wants her to stay on it.
o: Take the medicine one hour before meals
Stop the medicine on her own
Take the medicine one hour after meals
Take double the dose at night
patients.w: If a medicine contributes and cannot be stopped, take it one hour before meals, because eating stimulates saliva (T@88526 11/20).

x.Stop the medicine on her own: The point is to keep a medicine she cannot stop; she is not told to stop it herself.
x.Take the medicine one hour after meals: The advice is before meals, not after.
x.Take double the dose at night: Doubling a dose is not an advised step.

patients.t: A man with heart failure on a sodium-restricted diet asks about an artificial saliva.
o: Xylitol, a sugar alcohol sweetener
Isomalt, a sugar alcohol sweetener
Sodium carboxymethylcellulose
Glucose oxidase, an enzyme
patients.w: Sodium carboxymethylcellulose and sodium monofluorophosphate carry asterisks: avoid products with sodium on a sodium-restricted diet (slide 82).

x.Xylitol, a sugar alcohol sweetener: Xylitol is not a sodium compound.
x.Isomalt, a sugar alcohol sweetener: Isomalt is not a sodium compound.
x.Glucose oxidase, an enzyme: Glucose oxidase is not a sodium compound.

patients.t: A man has dry mouth with a fever, swollen lymph nodes and white patches on his tongue.
o: Artificial saliva gel and a recheck in 5-7 days
Chew sugar-free gum after every meal each day
Use a humidifier in the bedroom at night
Referral for fever, swollen lymph nodes and candidiasis
patients.w: Fever and swollen lymph nodes, and candidiasis, are exclusions to self-care in dry mouth (slide 79).

x.Artificial saliva gel and a recheck in 5: Artificial saliva is for patients without an exclusion.
x.Chew sugar-free gum after every meal eac: Sugar-free gum is a self-care step; he has exclusions.
x.Use a humidifier in the bedroom at night: A humidifier is a self-care step; he has exclusions.

patients.t: A patient used artificial saliva after meals and at bedtime for 6 days, and the dryness has lessened.
o: Stop all of the measures because the dryness lessened
Continue artificial saliva, fluoride and non-drug measures
Refer to the PCP for further evaluation of the dryness
Add a second artificial saliva product to the first
patients.w: When dryness lessened after 5-7 days of self-treatment, the patient continues artificial saliva, fluoride products and the non-drug measures (slide 84).

x.Stop all of the measures because the dry: Stopping leaves the dryness untreated; artificial saliva is replacement, not a cure.
x.Refer to the PCP for further evaluation: Referral is for dryness that worsens or new symptoms.
x.Add a second artificial saliva product t: Nothing in the case calls for a second product.

patients.t: A pharmacist gives instructions for an artificial saliva gel.
o: Use it only once a day at bedtime before sleeping
Rub a 1-inch ribbon of it on the gums after meals
Put 1/2 inch on the tongue and spread it through the mouth
Swallow a 1/2-inch length of it after each meal
patients.w: Place a 1/2-inch length of gel on the tongue and spread it thoroughly in the mouth; use at any time, at a minimum after all meals and before bed (slides 82-83).

x.Use it only once a day at bedtime before: The use is at any time, at a minimum after meals and before bed.
x.Rub a 1-inch ribbon of it on the gums af: The length is 1/2 inch and it goes on the tongue.
x.Swallow a 1/2-inch length of it after ea: It is spread in the mouth, not swallowed.

numbers: length of gel placed on the tongue
take a contributing medicine before meals

standard-fluoride.name: Standard fluoride toothpaste

la.text: First step for tooth hypersensitivity: a soft-bristle toothbrush with standard fluoride toothpaste for 7 days. She said it helps the surface of the enamel.

sk.text: Fluoride ions from toothpastes and gels (Na2PO3F, SnF2, NaF) convert enamel hydroxyapatite, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2, into fluorapatite, Ca10(PO4)6F2, which is more resistant to acid erosion; they also enhance mineral deposition. More than 2 mg/L can cause enamel fluorosis.

counsel: Use a soft-bristle (low-abrasion) toothbrush with the standard fluoride toothpaste for 7 days.
Do not brush for 30-60 minutes after acidic food or drinks.
If the pain is not better after one week, the next step is a desensitizing toothpaste.

how.text: Fluoride ions convert hydroxyapatite into fluorapatite, which resists acid erosion, and enhance mineral deposition (remineralization).

potassium-nitrate.name: Potassium nitrate 5% (desensitizing toothpaste)

la.text: Desensitizing toothpaste active: depolarizes the excited nerves in the tubules. Not for children under 12 years: children swallow toothpaste, with a higher risk of electrolyte problems.
la.src: Lam oral slide 15; handout p. 4; T@50194 11/20

counsel: A single application has no effect: use it continuously.
Apply a 1-inch strip to a soft-bristle brush and brush at least twice daily.
It may take 4-6 weeks to see the benefit; continue until the sensitivity subsides or as long as the dentist recommends.
See a dentist if pain persists or worsens, or new symptoms develop after 4-6 weeks.
potassium-nitrate.counselSrc: Lam oral slides 17, 18; handout p. 4; T@50656-T@51140 11/20

how.text: Depolarizes the excited nerves in the tubules.

sodium-fluoride.name: Sodium fluoride (desensitizing toothpaste)

la.text: Listed with potassium nitrate and stannous fluoride in the row that depolarizes the excited nerves in the tubules.

sk.text: Fluoride ions from toothpastes and gels (Na2PO3F, SnF2, NaF) convert enamel hydroxyapatite, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2, into fluorapatite, Ca10(PO4)6F2, which is more resistant to acid erosion; they also enhance mineral deposition. More than 2 mg/L can cause enamel fluorosis.

counsel: Same directions as every desensitizing toothpaste: 1-inch strip, at least twice daily, continuous use.

how.text: Depolarizes the excited nerves in the tubules (slide 15 row with potassium nitrate and stannous fluoride).

stannous-fluoride.name: Stannous fluoride (desensitizing toothpaste)

la.text: Listed with potassium nitrate and sodium fluoride in the row that depolarizes the excited nerves in the tubules.

sk.text: SnF2 is one of the fluoride sources on his slide 17; the fluoride ion converts hydroxyapatite into fluorapatite.

counsel: Same directions as every desensitizing toothpaste: 1-inch strip, at least twice daily, continuous use.

how.text: Depolarizes the excited nerves in the tubules (slide 15 row with potassium nitrate and sodium fluoride).

arginine.name: Arginine 8% (desensitizing toothpaste)

la.text: Desensitizing toothpaste active: minimizes the flow of fluid by sealing the exposed dentin. The handout prints arginine calcium; slide 15 prints arginine 8%.

counsel: Same directions as every desensitizing toothpaste: 1-inch strip, at least twice daily, continuous use.

how.text: Minimizes the flow of fluid by sealing the exposed dentin.

benzocaine-oral.name: Benzocaine (oral and lip anesthetic)

la.text: Canker sore: benzocaine 10-20% (slide 34; handout 5-20%), apply up to 4 times a day as needed, age over 2 years. Cold sore: 5-20% in the handout; her practice key counts benzocaine 5% gel, a thin layer 3-4 times after a meal, as right (she said plus or minus). It relieves pain only; it does not reduce the duration.
la.src: Lam oral slides 34, 54; handout pp. 7, 11; T@62128, T@84973 11/20

sk.text: A local anesthetic in gels or combination agents. Methemoglobinemia is rare but a concern: CYP enzymes convert benzocaine to benzocaine hydroxylamine.

counsel: Apply to the sore after meals, up to 4 times a day as needed (cold sore: a thin layer, 3-4 times a day).
Avoid eating or drinking for at least 30 minutes after application.
Do not combine with menthol, phenol or camphor: tissue irritation and damage.
avoid: Combination with menthol, phenol or camphor (tissue irritation)

benzyl-alcohol.name: Benzyl alcohol (oral anesthetic)

la.text: Canker sore: 0.05-0.1% (slide 34 and handout), apply up to 4 times a day as needed, age over 2 years. The handout's cold sore table prints 10-33%.

counsel: Apply to the sore up to 4 times a day as needed; avoid eating or drinking for 30 minutes.
Do not combine with menthol, phenol or camphor.
avoid: Combination with menthol, phenol or camphor

carbamide-peroxide-oral.name: Carbamide peroxide 10-15% (oral debriding agent)

la.text: Cleanses the sore and relieves discomfort. Direct application: apply to the area, leave 1 minute, spit out. Rinse: a few drops on the tongue, mix with saliva, swish 1 minute. She said 1 or 2 minutes for direct application aloud.
la.src: Lam oral slide 35; handout p. 7; T@63829 11/20

sk.text: Carbamide peroxide (10%) is used as a mouth rinse for canker sores.

counsel: Use after meals, 3-4 times a day.
Avoid eating or drinking for at least 30 minutes afterwards.
Use for up to 7 days: longer use lets opportunistic organisms grow (black hairy tongue); prolonged use causes tooth sensitivity and soft tissue irritation.
Patient with sensitive teeth: use direct application, not the rinse.
carbamide-peroxide-oral.counselSrc: Lam oral slide 36; handout p. 7; T@64264-T@65270 11/20

hydrogen-peroxide.name: Hydrogen peroxide 1.5% or 3% (oral debriding agent)

la.text: 1.5%: direct application to the sore, leave 1 minute, spit. 3%: swish for one minute (the handout adds: mix with an equal amount of water before rinsing). She mentioned a home-made 3% or 5% rinse and was unsure aloud.
la.src: Lam oral slide 35; handout p. 7; T@63359 11/20

counsel: Use after meals, 3-4 times a day; avoid eating or drinking for at least 30 minutes after.
Use for up to 7 days.
It can irritate enamel and soft tissue: with sensitive teeth, use the applicator, not the rinse.
avoid: Rinse in a patient with tooth hypersensitivity

protectant-disc.name: Oral protectant (paste, patch or dissolving disc)

la.text: Coats and protects the sore; a barrier forms and dissolves in 8-12 hours. Use up to 3-4 times a day after meals; avoid drinking for up to 30 minutes. Placement time: slide 37 prints 10-20 seconds; the handout and her speech say 10-20 minutes.
la.src: Lam oral slide 37; handout p. 8; T@65817 11/20

counsel: Place it against the sore long enough to adhere (slide 37: 10-20 seconds; handout and speech: 10-20 minutes).
It dissolves by itself in 8-12 hours; use up to 3-4 times a day after meals.
Avoid drinking for up to 30 minutes.
protectant-disc.counselSrc: Lam oral slide 37; handout p. 8; T@65817 11/20

saline-rinse.name: Saline rinse and baking soda paste

la.text: Saline: 1-3 teaspoons of salt in 4-8 ounces of warm water; any salt. Baking soda paste: apply to the lesion for a few minutes. Use up to 4 times a day. An antiseptic rinse such as Listerine is another option.
la.src: Lam oral slide 38; handout p. 8; T@66281-T@66756 11/20

sk.text: Listerine contains thymol, eucalyptol, methyl salicylate and menthol; sodium bicarbonate raises saliva pH and lowers growth of acidic bacteria.

counsel: Up to 4 times a day.
Use the saline rinse before topical applications of medicines (handout).

analgesic-oral-systemic.name: NSAIDs or acetaminophen (systemic analgesics)

la.text: For additional pain relief in canker sores and cold sores. Aspirin tablets are not held in the mouth or on the lesion: chemical burn with tissue damage.
la.src: Lam oral slides 39, 55; handout pp. 8, 11; T@69759, T@80499 11/20

counsel: Swallow the tablet; never hold aspirin against the sore.
avoid: Aspirin held in the mouth: chemical burn

docosanol.name: Docosanol 10% cream

la.text: First-line topical antiviral for a cold sore: reduces the duration and severity of symptoms. Apply at the first sign (prodrome), up to 5 times a day until the lesion heals, up to 10 days.
la.src: Lam oral slides 51-53; handout p. 11; T@78159-T@79314 11/20

counsel: Start at the first tingling or burning, before a blister: the earlier, the better.
Apply up to 5 times a day until the lesion heals; use for up to 10 days.
It still helps once the lesion is present.
Keep the sore clean, wash the hands often and keep the skin moist.

how.text: Inhibits direct fusion between the herpesvirus and the human cell plasma membrane, so the virus does not replicate (handout); she said it prevents the virus from attaching to the human cell.

camphor-menthol-hsl.name: Camphor and menthol (in topical analgesics)

la.text: In a cold sore, camphor above 3% and menthol above 1% are contraindicated: counterirritant effect; irritating at higher concentration. Vicks rub has about 5% camphor. In a canker sore, anesthetics are not combined with menthol, phenol or camphor.
la.src: Lam oral slides 34, 54; handout p. 11; T@79739-T@80226 11/20

avoid: Camphor above 3% in a cold sore
Menthol above 1% in a cold sore

triple-antibiotic-hsl.name: Triple antibiotic ointment

la.text: Only for a suspected secondary bacterial infection: the lesion is not forming a mature lesion, with no crusting, and is still red.
la.src: Lam oral slides 51, 56; handout p. 11; T@80604 11/20

counsel: Apply a thin layer 3-4 times a day.
Follow up with the PCP.

la.text: Do not recommend: the herpes virus does not respond to corticosteroids (HSL is not a steroid-responsive dermatosis), and topical steroids are highly astringent. Her practice key leaves hydrocortisone 1% ointment out.
la.src: Lam oral slide 58; handout p. 12; T@81857 11/20

complementary-hsl.name: Tea tree oil, lysine and zinc

la.text: Not enough data to justify use; the guidelines do not recommend them to prevent or treat cold sores. Handout: tea tree oil has some in vitro activity against HSV; lysine may reduce the frequency of outbreaks, data conflicting; zinc cream and aloe vera gel have shown some efficacy.
la.src: Lam oral slide 57; handout p. 11; T@81119-T@81468 11/20

artificial-saliva.name: Artificial saliva

la.text: Replacement therapy for dry mouth, not a cure: it lacks the protective components of the natural saliva. Sprays, gels, gums, toothpaste. Gel: place 1/2 inch on the tongue and spread it. Use at any time, at a minimum after meals and before bed. Ingredients: isomalt, xylitol, glucose oxidase, sodium carboxymethylcellulose*, sorbitol, sodium monofluorophosphate*; avoid * products on a sodium-restricted diet.
la.src: Lam oral slides 82, 83; handout p. 15; T@89229-T@90208 11/20

sk.text: Sodium monofluorophosphate (Na2PO3F) is one of the fluoride sources on his slide 17.

counsel: Gel: place a 1/2-inch length on the tongue and spread it through the mouth.
Use at any time; at a minimum after all meals and before going to bed.
Low-sodium diet: avoid products that contain sodium.
Evaluate after 5-7 days; continue artificial saliva, fluoride products and non-drug measures if the dryness lessened.
avoid: Products with sodium on a sodium-restricted diet (heart failure, high blood pressure)

dentin-tubules: Tiny fluid-filled channels in dentin through which sensation is transmitted to the pulp. When enamel is lost or the gum recedes they are open to the oral cavity and the pulp.
fluorapatite: Ca10(PO4)6F2, formed when fluoride replaces the hydroxide in hydroxyapatite; it is more resistant to acid erosion.
prodrome: Symptoms a patient may feel before the lesion appears, such as burning, tingling or itching.
latency: A herpesvirus infection that persists in the body without lesions and can reactivate later when a stimulus triggers it.
or-vesicle: A small fluid-containing blister; in a cold sore the fluid holds live virus.
or-astringent: The reason she gave against topical steroids on a cold sore: it irritates the skin.

tell.title: Cold sore or canker sore

path.q: Is the sore inside the mouth or on and around the lip?
a: Inside the mouth, a gray or yellow oval ulcer with a red halo → **canker sore**
On or around the lip → next question

path.q: Is it a red, fluid-filled lesion that merges and crusts?
a: No → reconsider the location and look

rows: Exact cause unknown; triggers such as local trauma, immune or nutritional conditions, medicines, stress
Herpes simplex virus 1, latent and reactivated by triggers
Inside the mouth: tongue, floor of the mouth, soft palate, inside the lips and cheeks; minor RAS: not the gingiva, hard palate or vermilion border
Junction of oral mucosa and skin of the lip and nose; she said outside the mouth or around the lips
Slide 47; the handout lists intraoral keratinized mucosa for HSL
Oval, flat ulcer; gray or yellow, crateriform when major; red tissue around it
Red, fluid-filled vesicles that coalesce; crusted when mature
A pricking or burning prodrome, 2-48 hours
Burning, itching, tingling or numbness, 2-48 hours
Resolves on its own in 7-14 days
No required order: anesthetic, debriding agent, protectant, rinse, systemic analgesic
Docosanol 10% first line, with or without an anesthetic; no topical steroid
More than 14 days; frequent recurrence; systemic illness; failed self-care; no relief after 7 days of a debriding agent
No previous diagnosis; more than 14 days; increased frequency; immunocompromised; systemic infection; recurrence

tell.title: Tooth hypersensitivity or toothache

path.q: Does the pain stay when nothing touches the tooth?
a: No, it comes with heat, cold, pressure or acid and stops → next question

path.q: Is the pain very severe, or are there other exclusions (swelling, loose teeth, bleeding gums)?

rows: Quick, fleeting, sharp or stabbing on exposure; stops when the stimulus is gone
Fluid in the tubules moves with the stimulus and stimulates the pulp nerves
Inflammatory response stimulates free nerve endings in the pulp; continuous, dull, throbbing pain usually means irreversible damage
Yes, if mild and no exclusion
Soft-bristle brush with standard fluoride 7 days, then a desensitizing toothpaste
None over the counter; the dentist cleans it out

pairs.title: Carbamide peroxide in the mouth or in the ear
a: Direct application: leave 1 minute, spit; or a few drops on the tongue, swish 1 minute; up to 7 days
b: 5-10 drops in the ear, several minutes, twice daily for up to four days

pairs.title: Hydrogen peroxide 1.5% or 3% in the mouth
a: Direct application to the sore, 1 minute, spit
b: Swish for one minute; handout: mixed with an equal amount of water first

pairs.title: Docosanol or benzocaine for a cold sore
